raw_response:
I will keep my farm anchored in the crops I trust most. In Quzhou, the land and climate fit wheat-maize very well, and I have well irrigation, so I will put most of my land into that rotation and protect steady grain output first. I am 58 and have farmed 40 years, so I do not want to scatter too much land into crops that need heavy hand labor, many spray rounds, or constant field checking. I will still keep some cotton, chrysanthemum, spinach, mungbean, and soybean, but I will hold them to smaller areas so I can manage them carefully instead of spreading myself thin.

I will use improved or hybrid seed where it matters for stand, yield, and uniformity. I will not chase very high fertilizer rates just because water is available. On my farm, that usually wastes money and can push weak growth or disease. For wheat and maize, I will feed enough for a solid yield and use irrigation at the key stages. For cotton and chrysanthemum, I will accept higher management intensity because they bring cash, but I will keep their area controlled. For mungbean and soybean, I will stay light on nitrogen because they can carry more of that load themselves. For spinach, I will use more water and more nitrogen because that crop pays through fast, tender leaf growth. I am making these choices around Quzhou’s wheat-maize system and local warm-temperate conditions with about 201 to 212 frost-free days and roughly 556 to 792 mm annual rainfall, with most rain in summer ([中国天气网](https://www.weather.com.cn/cityintro/101091015.shtml), [国家生态数据中心曲周站](https://www.nesdc.org.cn/otherProject/index?menuId=station&projectId=1097), [农业农村部转引河北新闻](https://www.moa.gov.cn/xw/qg/202107/t20210720_6372348.htm)).
